name: CRB-913
lead: CRB-913 is an investigational oral drug from Corbus Pharmaceuticals that blocks the cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) outside the brain, being developed for obesity. It is not approved for any use.[1][2][3] Its appearance relevance is through fat loss: reducing body fat gives a leaner body and a slimmer, more defined face, and drugs in this field are followed closely in physique and weight-loss communities.

In a 2023 paper in Obesity, researchers described CRB-913 as a CB1 inverse agonist with similar preclinical potency to rimonabant but markedly reduced brain penetration, and reported that in diet-induced obese mice it lowered body weight on its own and added to the weight loss of tirzepatide, semaglutide and liraglutide.[1] Rimonabant, an earlier CB1 blocker, was withdrawn over psychiatric effects, which is why brain exposure is a focus of the new compound's design.[1]

A Phase 1b trial (NCT07310901, called CANYON-1) enrolled 254 adults with obesity and no diabetes at 15 US sites, double-blind and placebo-controlled, with 12 weeks of daily dosing.[2][3] A press report dated September 2026 says the highest dose studied produced a least-squares mean weight loss of 5.0% at week 12, against none on placebo, with each dose significantly better than placebo, and that discontinuation due to adverse events ranged from 3.1% to 13.1%.[3]

paras: CRB-913 is described as a CB1 receptor inverse agonist. In mice it showed 3.8-fold larger plasma exposure and 9.5-fold lower brain levels than rimonabant.[1] The CB1 receptor is considered a clinically validated target in obesity, and several experimental CB1 inverse agonists have been shown to induce weight loss.[1]

The Phase 1b study (NCT07310901) enrolled 254 participants and began on 4 December 2025; the registry lists it as completed.[2] According to a press report, adults without diabetes were randomised across three daily doses and placebo for 12 weeks with 4 weeks of follow-up; weight loss at week 12 was 2.8%, 3.3% and 5.0% across the three doses versus 0% on placebo.[3] The report says no serious or severe psychiatric events or suicidality occurred, one moderate transient depressive symptom case was reported among 188 participants on active drug, and irritability was the most common psychiatric event.[3] Comparisons with oral GLP-1 drugs are cross-trial rather than head-to-head.[3]

In diet-induced obese mice, CRB-913 monotherapy produced a dose-dependent decrease in body weight, reaching -22% within 18 days, and in combination with tirzepatide, semaglutide or liraglutide reduced body weight by 32.6%, 28.8% and 16.8% by day 18, with improvements in body fat content and liver measures.[1] Mouse findings do not establish effects in humans.

timeline.event: Mouse study of CRB-913 with incretin drugs published.[1]

card.summary: An experimental CB1 blocker that boosted GLP-1 drugs in obese mice; human data are not yet public.
card.note: Investigational; mouse data only published so far.

quick.overview:
CRB-913 is an experimental drug that blocks the CB1 receptor, with the aim of aiding weight loss. In mice it added to the effects of GLP-1-type drugs.

A Phase 1b human trial is listed as completed, but no results have been found.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor linked to appetite and metabolism, and is described as peripherally acting.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not public. The earlier CB1 blocker rimonabant was withdrawn over psychiatric effects; whether CRB-913 shares them is untested in published work.

chain: Blocks CB1 receptors outside the brain
angle.text: If approved, a peripheral CB1 blocker would act on weight and body fat, the route by which people hope to look leaner. Human results so far come from a 12-week early-phase trial.
